cases.title: Nigeria 2020 electricity tariff rise under World Bank power loan
cases.point: Abuja, seat of the federal government and the electricity regulator NERC; the tariff rise applied nationwide

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Approved a US$750 million IDA credit, the Power Sector Recovery Operation, on 23 June 2020. Money is paid out only when agreed results are met. One required result (DLI #3) is that end-user tariffs are raised in line with a plan to remove tariff shortfalls. A further package followed in 2021 and additional financing in 2023.

cases.conditions: World Bank Program-for-Results loan (P164001). Two 'global' results must be met before any other money is paid: the regulator sets company revenue needs through tariff reviews, and the government adopts and funds a plan to cover and then eliminate tariff shortfalls. Standard result DLI #3 requires end-user tariffs to be adjusted in line with the financing plan, including its measures to protect the poor. Households using under 50 kWh a month kept a protected tariff (World Bank project paper, 2023).
cases.community: In 2019 tariffs covered only 56% of cost, and the government paid a shortfall of ₦581 billion (US$1.6 billion). A July 2020 tariff review planned a 46% rise from September 2020; a 38% rise took effect in November 2020. By February 2022 tariffs reached 96.4% of cost (World Bank, 2023). The Bretton Woods Project said most Nigerians would pay more for power, in a year when the economy shrank 6.1% in the second quarter. The same month the government also ended petrol subsidies (Reuters).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The Nigeria Labour Congress called an indefinite general strike over the petrol and power price rises from 28 September 2020. Reuters reported that Nigeria faced pressure from lenders such as the World Bank 'to qualify for budget support loans.' The unions suspended the strike after the government agreed to hold off the tariff rise for two weeks while a committee chaired by Labour Minister Festus Keyamo reviewed it. The 38% rise then took effect in November 2020. The World Bank credits that rise as the main reason tariffs neared full cost.

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's own project paper ties loan payments to tariff adjustments and counts the 38% rise as a result. The size of the rise per household is not given in these sources.

cases.title: Sale of Nigeria's state power company (NEPA/PHCN)
cases.point: Abuja, where the Bureau of Public Enterprises ran the sale and the Abuja distribution company was handed over (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Privatization Support Project (IDA credit, US$114.29 million, 2001) paid advisers to break up NEPA into separate companies, design the power market and tariff rules, and run the sale of the generation and distribution companies. The World Bank says the 2010 power strategy carried out the privatization plan developed with this project's support.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Under the 2005-2007 Policy Support Instrument, Nigeria listed among outstanding benchmarks the bid opening for concessioning the Transmission Company of Nigeria before the final IMF Board review (letter of intent, September 2007).

cases.conditions: World Bank Privatization Support Project components: corporate restructuring of NEPA, 'privatization of entities formed from NEPA', and a tariff strategy (World Bank completion report, 2011). IMF Policy Support Instrument: the government committed to complete 'bid opening for concessioning of Transmission Company of Nigeria' before the final IMF Board review (Nigeria letter of intent, 26 September 2007).

companies.name: KANN Consortium
companies.role: Took over the Abuja Electricity Distribution Company in November 2013 (Daily Trust).

companies.name: Manitoba Hydro International
companies.role: Given management control of the Transmission Company of Nigeria (Daily Trust).

cases.community: On 1 November 2013 ten distribution and four generation companies passed to private owners. Daily Trust reported that new owners disengaged staff at most plants. The electricity workers' union NUEE said more than 50,000 former PHCN staff were still owed entitlements and over 5,000 had received nothing (Guardian Nigeria). In 2019 the union said over 2,000 disengaged staff had not been paid since 2013, that the new distribution companies paid some workers half salaries, and that some did not pass on pension deductions (TheCable). A new tariff order (MYTO 2) in June 2013 raised bills (Daily Trust).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The union struck in early October 2013 over unpaid severance; an agreement to pay by end-November was signed. In December 2019 the union struck again over unpaid benefits, causing hours of blackouts, and called it off within 24 hours after government intervention (TheCable). Transmission stayed in state hands under a management contract.

cases.title: Nigeria port concessions and dock job cuts
cases.point: Apapa, Lagos, Nigeria's main port (approximate; the concessions covered ports nationwide)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Privatization Support Project (IDA credit, US$114.29 million, 2001) supported the port reform. The World Bank lists port concessions (US$115 million) among the sales achieved under the project.

cases.conditions: Privatization Support Project: advisory and institutional support to the Bureau of Public Enterprises for privatizations and concessions, including the ports (World Bank completion report, 2011).
cases.community: The World Bank's own completion report records that over 5,000 Nigerian Ports Authority staff were 'disengaged', with over ₦20 billion paid in entitlements, severance and pension buyouts. Casual dock labourers were cut from about 13,000 to about 3,000. The report calls labour retrenchment the most difficult part of the port reform.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the source.
cases.outcome: The World Bank counts shorter ship waiting times (from 14-21 days to 0-1 day) as gains. It presents the port reform as a model for other West African countries.

sources.title: Nigeria - Privatization Support Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report

cases.confidence_note: Only one source, the lender's own report, gives the job figures. Concession holders are not named in it.

cases.title: Sale of Eleme Petrochemicals
cases.point: Eleme petrochemical plant near Port Harcourt (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Lists the Eleme sale (US$225 million, 11.9% of all proceeds) among privatizations achieved under its Privatization Support Project. Its private arm, the IFC, lent US$75 million and mobilised US$80 million for the buyer (Bretton Woods Project).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The Bretton Woods Project says the sale was listed as a structural reform under the IMF Policy Support Instrument in October 2005.

cases.conditions: World Bank Privatization Support Project (2001-2010) financed the privatization programme that sold Eleme (World Bank completion report, 2011). The IMF Policy Support Instrument's reform list included sales of state assets (Bretton Woods Project, 2008).

companies.name: Indorama Group
companies.role: Buyer; reportedly received a 75% stake against a memorandum that set a 51/49 split (Bretton Woods Project).
companies.hq: Indonesia (as stated by Bretton Woods Project)

cases.community: The National Union of Petroleum and Natural Gas Workers (NUPENG) said the plant was undervalued. The Bretton Woods Project reports that staff fell from 1,000 to 296 after the sale.
cases.suppression: The Bretton Woods Project reports that troops took the plant by force for the handover.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Indorama ran the plant. A House of Representatives investigation of privatizations followed in March 2008 (Bretton Woods Project).

cases.title: Maputo water lease (Águas de Moçambique)
cases.point: Maputo, centre of the 15-year lease area (management contracts also covered Beira, Quelimane, Nampula and Pemba)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: IDA credit 3247 for the Second National Water Development Project (1999) required the lease and management contracts to be signed before the credit could take effect, and set a full-cost-recovery tariff policy as a key indicator. IDA added a US$15 million supplemental credit in 2004 to cover higher contract costs.

cases.conditions: Development Credit Agreement, Section 6.01(e): a condition for the credit to take effect was that the asset fund FIPAG had signed 'the Lease Contract and the Management Contract' with the winning bidder for Maputo, Beira, Quelimane, Nampula and Pemba (World Bank, 1999). A key project indicator was a tariff policy based on full cost recovery (World Bank completion report, 2009).

companies.name: SAUR International
companies.role: Lead shareholder of the operator Águas de Moçambique; quit the contracts in December 2001 and sold its share for €1.

companies.name: Águas de Portugal
companies.role: Took over the operator after SAUR left.

cases.community: The World Bank expected customers with connections to pay higher tariffs. After SAUR left, the contracts were renegotiated: the operator's rate rose and costs went up by about US$8.5 million, plus US$7.15 million to cover deficits in four cities. A 2006 survey found the share of peri-urban Maputo residents supplied by the operator fell from about 86% (2001) to 63% (2006). The share relying on small private vendors, who charge much higher prices, doubled. The operator was persistently late paying lease fees to the public asset fund FIPAG.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: New contracts took effect in June 2004. Connections in Maputo rose from 77,793 (2000) to 109,932 (2009). FIPAG drew on the operator's US$400,000 security in December 2007 over unpaid fees. The World Bank rated the operator's performance unsatisfactory four times after SAUR's exit.

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank links the fall in coverage partly to fast urban growth and the decline of public standpipes, not only to the lease.

cases.title: Sale of Ghana's state gold mines at Tarkwa
cases.point: Tarkwa gold mine, Wassa West District (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project (IDA credit 1921, 1988) paid to restructure the State Gold Mining Corporation (SGMC) and to attract buyers. The World Bank says the credit helped bring about the sale of SGMC's three mines, including Tarkwa. It also funded the start of the 1986 Minerals and Mining Law.

cases.conditions: Under the Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project, the government and lenders agreed to fund the work needed to attract investors and sell all of SGMC's mines, with cost cutting and downsizing at SGMC (World Bank completion report, 1997).

companies.name: Gold Fields
companies.role: Took over the Tarkwa mine in July 1993 and later converted it to surface mining.

cases.community: Earthworks reports that mining displaced 30,000 people in the Wassa area between 1990 and 1998 (it does not say who counted). It says land was taken from farmers 'often using force and without adequate compensation'. On 16 October 2001 a cyanide spill at Gold Fields' Tarkwa mine left more than 1,000 people without drinking water and affected at least five villages. Researcher William Tsuma (2010) describes community displacement as regular after the move to surface mining.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: SGMC was dissolved by March 1997. Tarkwa output rose from 20,528 ounces (1989) to 47,450 ounces (1996). The World Bank rated the project highly satisfactory. The village of Abekoase reached an out-of-court settlement with the mining company in December 2003 (Earthworks).

sources.title: Ghana - Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project: Implementation Completion Report
Tarkwa, Ghana
Mining-Sector Reforms in Ghana: Institutionalizing and Legitimizing Large-Scale Land Deals

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank documents its role in the sale. The 30,000 displacement figure covers all mines in the Wassa area, not only Tarkwa, and Earthworks does not name who counted it.

cases.title: Kazakhstan pension privatization
cases.point: Almaty, the capital when the 1997 pension law was passed (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Pension Reform Adjustment Loan (PRAL), US$300 million in three tranches, effective June 1998, with 19 conditions before Board approval, 8 for the second tranche and 9 for the third. It supported the move from a pay-as-you-go system to private individual accounts. The third tranche was cancelled for two unmet conditions.

cases.conditions: The PRAL supported the June 1997 pension law that replaced the state pay-as-you-go system with fully funded individual accounts paid into competing private funds (10% of earnings), and set tranche conditions on its implementation (World Bank President's Report, 1998; IEG evaluation, 2007). A parallel Asian Development Bank loan (US$100 million, 1997) had 41 policy conditions, including enrolling at least 60% of formal-sector workers.
cases.community: The replacement rate (pension as a share of pay) fell from 60% before the reform to 29.3% in 2013. Coverage fell from about 66% of the labour force to 63%. Fees were estimated to take 16.8% of an account's final balance after 40 years (ILO, 2018). A World Bank study projected replacement rates of about 23% for women and just over 40% for men (Asian Development Bank completion report). The retirement age was raised from 60 to 63 for men and 55 to 58 for women. The IMF estimated the 1998-2025 transition cost at 36.5% of 1997 GDP.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: In 2013 Kazakhstan created a Unified Pension Fund, which the ILO describes as practically reversing the privatization. The World Bank's own evaluation says the accounts are unlikely to give adequate pensions to many people, especially women and those with broken careers.

cases.title: Hungary 1998 pension privatization

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Granted a one-tranche Public Sector Adjustment Loan (PSAL) of US$150 million. Its policy matrix, the conditions for Board presentation, included adopting a new mandatory private pension pillar and cutting public pension terms. An earlier US$132 million pension and health administration loan also supported the reform.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The ILO says the IMF and World Bank recommended pension privatization and soon dominated the reform debate.

cases.conditions: PSAL policy actions: 'New multi-pillar system adopted', mandatory for new labour-force entrants; retirement age raised from 55 (women) and 60 (men) to 62; indexation changed from net wages to a mixed wage/price formula; private fund rules acceptable to the World Bank (World Bank IEG Hungary evaluation, 2007).
cases.community: Pensions in the privatized system were estimated to be 9.8-12.5% lower than before for people with 20 years of contributions and over 18% lower with 30 years. Coverage fell from about 75% of the labour force (1998) to 71.8% (2009). Fund fees took 14.5% of contributions in 2007. Transition costs rose from 0.3% of GDP in 1998 to 1.2% in 2010 (ILO, 2018).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Act CI of October 2010 moved private pension savings back to the state system. The government used 243 billion forints of the transferred assets to repay an IMF loan. The IMF, World Bank, EU and OECD criticized the reversal (ILO, 2018).

sources.title: Hungary - Pension reform and the development of pension systems: an evaluation of World Bank assistance
Reversing Pension Privatizations: Rebuilding public pension systems in Eastern Europe and Latin America
sources.publisher: International Labour Organization (Ortiz, Durán-Valverde, Urban, Wodsak, eds.)

cases.confidence_note: Parliament passed the pension laws in 1996-1997; the World Bank evaluation says the PSAL conditions were to be met before the loan was granted.

cases.title: Bolivia 1997 pension privatization
cases.point: La Paz, seat of government (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Capitalization Program Adjustment Credit (CPAC) made approval of a pension law a condition for releasing the financial-sector tranche. A parallel Inter-American Development Bank loan had identical conditions.

cases.conditions: CPAC tranche conditions included '(i) approval of a pension law providing for reform of the existing funds' and setting up accounts to distribute shares from the capitalization (sale) of state firms (World Bank IEG Bolivia evaluation, 2007).
cases.community: Coverage stayed at about 12% of the labour force, the lowest in Latin America. Pensions averaged about 20% of average working-life pay. The share of older women receiving any pension fell from 23.7% to 12.8% between 1995 and 2007. Administrative costs were about 18% of contributions in 2004. Transition costs were 2.5 times the first estimates (ILO, 2018).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Law No. 065 of 10 December 2010 replaced the private system with a public pay-as-you-go system (ILO, 2018).

sources.title: Bolivia - Pension reform and the development of pension systems: an evaluation of World Bank assistance
Reversing Pension Privatizations: Rebuilding public pension systems in Eastern Europe and Latin America

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank evaluation names the pension law as a tranche condition; it also says the first draft law was prepared by Bolivian officials in 1993.

cases.title: Serbia 2015 state firm bankruptcies under IMF programme
cases.point: Belgrade, seat of the Privatization Agency (firms were spread across Serbia)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Stand-By Arrangement approved 23 February 2015 (about €1.2 billion). In its policy memorandum the government committed to resolve over 500 firms by sale or bankruptcy, and ending state aid to the Železara Smederevo steelworks was a prior action.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The government said it would start bankruptcies on the basis of an agreement with the World Bank (IMF Country Report 15/50).

cases.conditions: Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies, para. 29: the government committed to resolve over 500 Privatization Agency firms 'through either privatization or bankruptcy'. An action plan for bankruptcy of 188 companies was adopted in early February 2015. Para. 30: eliminate all state aid to Železara Smederevo (prior action) (IMF Country Report 15/50).
cases.community: Reuters reported about 5,000 job losses from the planned bankruptcy of the 188 firms. By mid-2016, about 300 firms employing about 25,000 workers had been liquidated, merged or sold. Five firms declared 'strategic', including Zastava vozila in Kragujevac, went bankrupt. The Heinrich Böll Foundation found no record of large severance payments in the budget.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: About 250 firms with about 55,000 workers were still unresolved in July 2016, and 11 strategic firms with about 21,000 workers remained (Heinrich Böll Foundation).

sources.title: Republic of Serbia: 2014 Article IV Consultation and Request for Stand-By Arrangement (Country Report No. 15/50)

cases.title: Oltchim privatization and insolvency

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: A draft letter of intent agreed with the IMF in 2011 committed Romania to sell Oltchim, with a tender by end-2011 and liquidation if the sale failed (Mediafax; Ziarul Financiar). Oltchim was one of 20 loss-making state firms monitored under the IMF arrangement. In January 2013 an IMF mission named it among state firms needing urgent action to avoid bankruptcy (Radio Romania International).

cases.conditions: Draft IMF letter of intent (agreed 3 May 2011): appoint a legal adviser by end-June 2011 and an investment bank by end-September 2011, complete the tender by end-2011; if the sale failed by end-2011, 'the firm will be placed in liquidation' (Ziarul Financiar). The state owned 54.79% (Mediafax).
cases.community: The 2012 sale went to businessman Dan Diaconescu, who did not pay the €45 million he promised. Workers' pay was delayed in late 2012. The firm entered insolvency in January 2013 with about 3,000 workers and output at 12% of capacity. In March 2013 over 1,000 workers protested three months of unpaid wages, and about 500 blocked traffic in Râmnicu Vâlcea and Pitești. Debt exceeded €620 million (Romania Insider).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: A court approved insolvency in late January 2013. Romania Insider, citing unnamed sources, reported the prime minister concluded after talks with the IMF that insolvency was the main way to ease a sale. Layoffs were planned as part of restructuring; the number was not yet known.

cases.title: Ukraine 2015 coal subsidy cut and miners' unpaid wages
cases.point: Novovolynsk state coal mines, site of 2016 hunger strike (protests also in Kyiv)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Extended Fund Facility approved March 2015. The programme's 2015 budget eliminated subsidies to coal mining and cut subsidies to state firms by 1.1% of GDP. The Kyiv Post describes the cut as 'a stipulation' of the 2015 IMF loan.

cases.conditions: Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies: the government 'eliminated price subsidies to the coal-mining industry' (worth 0.6% of GDP in 2014) as part of the 2015 budget (IMF Country Report 15/69).
cases.community: On 28 January 2015 about 1,500 miners picketed the Cabinet of Ministers in Kyiv. Wage arrears stood at UAH 600 million (US$38 million), with some unpaid since August 2014. The union warned over 50,000 jobs were at risk (IndustriALL). In 2016 a state plan aimed to support only about a third of 35 state mines, close or sell the rest and cut about 10,000 jobs (20%). Miners were owed three months' pay (Kyiv Post).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: On 7 November 2016, 50 workers at the No. 10 Novovolynska mine began a hunger strike; earlier, 300 people from the mine blocked the Yahodyn checkpoint on the Polish border. The energy minister promised all wage debts would be paid by January 2017. The 2017 budget set coal support at UAH 1.8 billion, against the union's demand of UAH 4.6 billion.

sources.title: Ukraine: Request for Extended Arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility (Country Report No. 15/69)

cases.confidence_note: The war in eastern Ukraine also cut coal output and subsidies. The January 2015 protest came after the budget passed but before the IMF approved the new programme in March 2015.
